Lessons.Title: Understanding Decay
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: explain fractional decrease as repeated multiplication by a remaining fraction, distinguish the amount lost from the amount retained, and compare a constant-factor decay with subtraction of a fixed amount. First-party Edulytiks adaptation of Illustrative Mathematics Algebra 1 First Edition Unit 5 Lesson 4, https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/teachers/1/5/4/preparation.html and student lesson https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/students/1/5/4/index.html (CC BY 4.0). The source uses the idea that losing a fraction leaves a complementary fraction.

Original fictional used-laptop depreciation: starting advertised value $640, losing25% of its CURRENT value each year. Remaining multiplier is1−0.25=0.75, so V(t)=640(0.75)^t for whole years t≥0. Values are $640,$480,$360,$270 at years0–3. Losses are $160,$120,$90 respectively: absolute dollar losses shrink while percent lost remains25%.

Contrast a different model subtracting a fixed $160 every year: 640,480,320,160; it matches the first decay model only at t0 and1, then diverges. If the original problem were 'lose $160 per year', repeated subtraction would be appropriate. The exact wording and reference amount matter.

Student task: explain algebraically why x decreased by one quarter gives x(3/4), extend a table and graph both models on same axes, and interpret when a physical amount would make an indefinite model implausible. Teacher-scored rubric 0–2 each for remaining-fraction derivation, correct values, model contrast and contextual limitations.

KeyConcepts.Title: Decay factor
KeyConcepts.Definition: For a fractional decrease r between0 and1, multiplier is1−r.

KeyConcepts.Title: Constant percentage versus amount
KeyConcepts.Definition: A constant percentage loss yields changing absolute losses.
KeyConcepts.Example: Losses160,120,90 while percent is25% each year.

KeyConcepts.Title: Positive exponential model
KeyConcepts.Definition: With a>0 and 0<b<1, a·b^t decreases while staying positive.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Identify initial a and multiplier b.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compute successive decay
WorkedExamples.Question: Find values at years1,2,3 for starting640 and 25% yearly loss.
WorkedExamples.Method: Investigate the first-party growth/decay table and independently check differences, ratios, exponents, and context.
Steps: Check each ratio to previous equals0.75.
WorkedExamples.Check: Multiplying all years by same0.75 factor.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compare percent and dollar decrease
WorkedExamples.Question: Why do year-to-year dollar losses change?
WorkedExamples.Method: Investigate the first-party growth/decay table and independently check differences, ratios, exponents, and context.
Steps: Each is 25% of that year's previous amount, not of initial640.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compare repeated subtraction
WorkedExamples.Question: What is value at t2 if $160 is removed each year?
WorkedExamples.Method: Investigate the first-party growth/decay table and independently check differences, ratios, exponents, and context.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Constant subtraction model t2=$320; decay-factor model t2=$360.
WorkedExamples.Check: The paths match at t1 but diverge thereafter.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Multiplying by0.25 instead of0.75 after a25% loss
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: 0.25 is the LOST fraction, not retained.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Subtracting25% of the original every year
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: This creates a different linear pattern.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating hypothetical price drop as a market forecast
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Actual depreciation need not follow a fixed factor.

SummaryPoints: Fractional decay is repeated multiplication by the retained fraction.
Dollar losses shrink even when percent decrease remains fixed.
Teacher reviews model reasoning and limitations.

Visuals.Title: First-party growth and decay observation table
Visuals.Description: Original hypothetical values calculated from exact models, not real scientific or financial measurements.
